summary: A humorous April 1st RFC that proposes adding a Death flag to TCP, using one bit in the header, to make TCP session narratives smooth and attractive. It is a joke and not a real protocol change.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9401 is an April 1st joke about adding a Death flag to TCP. It would signal that a session may end soon, but the document is not a real TCP change.

subtitle: An April 1st joke proposes a TCP flag for an approaching dramatic ending.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke imagines that TCP peers need a way to signal that a session is likely to end soon.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes a Death flag using the fourth control bit in a TCP header. A peer could send it before likely session termination.
tldr.outcome: The flag is described as informational and as not changing sequence or acknowledgment numbers. The narrative premise is humor, not a real TCP change.

today: RFC 9401 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2023. Its proposed TCP Death flag is humorous and does not change the TCP specification.

sections.title: A Flag for a Session's Ending
sections.content: This April 1st RFC proposes a Death flag, or DTH, to indicate likely termination of a TCP session. The name comes from “death flags” in anime, manga, and light novels: hints that a character will die soon. The document uses this narrative idea as its premise.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke borrows “death flags” from fiction. It proposes a TCP signal that a session may soon end.

sections.title: The Proposed Header Bit
sections.content: The proposed DTH flag occupies the fourth flag bit in the TCP control bits field. RFC 9401 says the flag is informational, does not change sequence or acknowledgment numbers, and does not require acknowledgment. A recipient need not act on it and should wait for a RST or FIN before closing the socket.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal puts DTH in the fourth control-bit position. It says the flag does not change TCP sequence handling or require an acknowledgment.

sections.title: When the Joke Says to Send It
sections.content: The RFC gives deliberately dramatic examples of when a peer might send DTH, such as when an application has resource problems or when a character reveals a hidden identity. It permits sending from either client or server and says the flag may be omitted even when termination is likely.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples connect network events to dramatic story endings. The RFC also says a sender may choose not to send the flag.
